clinicalPearls: The archetypal delusional misidentification syndrome, in which the patient believes a familiar person (often spouse or parent) has been replaced by an identical-looking imposter or double
The face is recognised as looking correct, but the sense of familiarity or emotional connection is absent, producing the conviction of substitution
May also extend to pets, objects, or places believed to have been duplicated or replaced
Classically described in schizophrenia and mood disorders but increasingly recognised in organic disease, including dementia (especially Lewy body), stroke, and traumatic brain injury
Right hemisphere and frontal dysfunction are frequently implicated, and organic causes should always be excluded
Can carry a risk of aggression directed at the supposed imposter
Management targets the underlying psychiatric or neurological disorder, with antipsychotics used for the delusional content
reference.pathophysiology: Capgras syndrome is a delusional misidentification thought to arise from a disconnection between intact facial recognition and the affective response that normally accompanies recognition of a familiar person. Damage to or dysfunction of pathways linking face-processing regions (fusiform cortex) with limbic structures (amygdala) that assign emotional significance leaves the face recognised but stripped of its felt familiarity. The mismatch is then rationalised as the person being an imposter. Right frontal and temporoparietal dysfunction, impairing belief evaluation and self-monitoring, is proposed to allow the aberrant belief to be maintained. It occurs in both primary psychiatric illness and a range of neurodegenerative and structural brain disorders.
additionalDifferentials: Fregoli syndrome (belief that strangers are a familiar persecutor in disguise)
Lewy body and other dementias with misidentification
additionalInvestigations: Cognitive assessment to detect underlying dementia or focal deficits
Neuroimaging (MRI brain) to identify right hemisphere, frontal, or degenerative changes
Bloods and metabolic screen to exclude reversible organic causes
Electroencephalography where delirium or seizures are considered
Psychiatric evaluation for a primary psychotic or mood disorder
redFlags: Threats or violence directed at the misidentified person
Abrupt onset with fluctuating consciousness suggesting delirium or acute brain lesion
Rapid cognitive decline pointing to a neurodegenerative process
Focal neurological signs indicating structural pathology
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the underlying cause; delusions accompanying treatable psychiatric illness may resolve with therapy, whereas those due to progressive dementia tend to persist or recur. The associated risk of harm to the misidentified individual requires active safety planning.
pitfalls: Assuming a purely psychiatric cause and missing an organic or neurodegenerative disorder
Overlooking the risk of violence toward the supposed imposter
Confusing Capgras with prosopagnosia or with Fregoli syndrome
Failing to reassess cognition over time as dementia may declare itself later
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
Kaplan and Sadock's Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry
management: Identify and treat the underlying cause, whether a primary psychiatric illness or an organic or neurodegenerative disorder
Antipsychotic therapy to target the delusional misidentification, choosing agents cautiously where Lewy body dementia is suspected because of neuroleptic sensitivity
Treat any underlying mood disorder or primary psychosis with appropriate antidepressant or mood-stabilising therapy
Cholinesterase inhibitors and dementia-directed care where a neurodegenerative cause is confirmed
Active safety planning to protect the misidentified individual given the risk of directed aggression
Psychological support and carer education, avoiding direct confrontation of the delusion
Multidisciplinary neuropsychiatry input with structured cognitive and neurological follow-up
